MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
For
USAID Asia Open RAN Academy
Between
the United States Agency for International Development
and
Telecom Infra Project
Purpose
1. This memorandum of understanding ("MOU") is entered into on July 8, 2022 ("Effective
Date") by and between Telecom Infra Project, a 501(c)(6) non-profit organization made
up of a global community of companies and organizations working together to accelerate
the development and deployment of open, interoperable, disaggregated, and
standards-based technology solutions, having its office at 401 Edgewater Place, Suite
600, Wakefield, Massachusetts 01880 (hereinafter referred to as "TIP", which
expression, unless it be repugnant to the meaning or context thereof, includes its
successors and permitted assigns) and United States Agency for International
Development, an independent Federal Government Agency, having its office at 1300
Pennsylvania Avenue, NW, Washington, DC 20523 (hereinafter referred to as "USAID",
which expression, unless it be repugnant to the meaning or context thereof, includes its
successors and permitted assigns). Each also hereinafter referred to individually as a
"Participant" and collectively as the "Participants".
2. By working together at both the strategic and operational levels, the Participants hope to
extend the impact and increase the efficiency of their programs and thus achieve better
measurable development outcomes. USAID and TIP are committed to working towards
the proliferation and adoption of open network architectures in the international
telecommunications sector to encourage increased supplier diversity and open, secure,
interoperable, and reliable digital ecosystems. The purpose of this MOU is to establish an
alliance between USAID and TIP to further the shared goals and objectives outlined
below, and to establish clear expectations and roles ("Collaboration"). This Memorandum
of Understanding (MOU) articulates the commonalities between the Participants'
objectives and approaches, and establishes a basis for ongoing dialogue and cooperation
between the Participants.
Participants
3. USAID is an independent Federal Government Agency that receives overall foreign-
policy guidance from the Secretary of State for the United States. USAID funds
international development that advances U.S. strategic objectives by improving economic
growth, food security, global health, democracy and governance; addressing
environmental and climate issues; and providing humanitarian assistance. USAID
finances development activities in Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Latin America, the
Caribbean, Europe, and Eurasia.

4. TIP is a global not-for-profit company founded in 2016 that includes hundreds of
companies, from service providers and technology partners to systems integrators and
other connectivity stakeholders. TIP and its members work together to develop,
test,validate, promote, and deploy open, interoperable, and disaggregated solutions that
deliver the high quality connectivity that the world needs.
Goals and Objectives
5. The Participants have the following strategic goals and objectives in common:
• USAID and TIP intend to collaborate in the Asia region to promote the
proliferation of open, interoperable, disaggregated, and standards-based
telecommunications networks that encourage increased supplier diversity in the
telecommunications sector. As part of USAID's International Open RAN
Initiative, USAID is piloting a workforce development program, the Asia Open
Radio Access Network (O-RAN) Academy, in the Philippines to support the skills
acquisition needed by current and future telecommunication sector workforce.
• TIP endeavors to bring its experience in the Open RAN space as well as leverage
the expertise of its participant companies to (1) share lessons learned and
perspectives on pertinent concepts to include in the Asia O-RAN Academy's
curriculum, (2) share potential opportunities to partner with TIP and its
participants, and (3) to engage with the private sector in the Philippines.
• This Collaboration between the Participants demonstrates a model for
public-private partnership that is designed for long-term success, replicability,
scale, and effectiveness in opening up the telecommunications infrastructure
market and promoting open, secure, interoperable, and reliable
telecommunications networks in our partner countries by encouraging supplier
diversity, with the aim to inspire additional public-private sector projects globally.
• In this partnership, USAID and TIP intend to work together to:
• Exchange non-confidential, non-proprietary information on the latest open
network architecture advances to help identify relevant and applicable
concepts to be included in the Asia O-RAN Academy curriculum for the
Philippines.
• Support TIP's efforts to develop, test and deploy open, interoperable,
disaggregated, and standards-based solutions that deliver high quality
connectivity in the Asia Region and beyond
Discuss ways to utilize opportunities for joint marketing and support the
work being done within each organization around Open RAN.
Roles and Responsibilities
6. Under this MOU, USAID intends to accomplish the following:
2

• Facilitate communication and information sharing between TIP, USAID Mission
and other U.S. Government staff in the field, host- country governments, and
implementing partners and non-governmental organizations in this regard, and
• Provide its technical expertise, support monitoring, and evaluation expertise so as
to share its learnings from the Asia O-RAN Academy and other USAID
International Open RAN Initiative programs;
• Promote adoption of Open RAN to increase network interoperability and security
in the Philippines through USAID's Better Access and Connectivity (BEACON)
actıvity.
• Promote TIP to government and industry partners
• Collaborate and provide regular read-outs of its initiatives to TIP and mutually
explore opportunities to publicize and generate awareness of one another's open
network architecture training opportunities and initiatives.
• Collaborate with Telkom University, as the TIP Community Lab host in the
Indo-Pacific region, to support the implementation of capacity building programs.
7. TIP intends to accomplish the following:
• Provide technical expertise for the curriculum design for the Asia O-RAN
Academy and promote the importance of open, interoperable, disaggregated, and
standards-based solutions that deliver high-quality connectivity in the Philippines
and the Asia region.
• Promote the Asia O-RAN Academy to its members and partners, to the extent that
its offerings do not duplicate those offered by TIP.
• Collaborate and provide regular read-outs of its initiatives to USAID and
mutually explore opportunities to publicize and generate awareness of one
another's open network architecture training opportunities and initiatives.
Implementation
8. To achieve the above-stated objectives, the Participants agree to meet as needed in order
to develop a mutually-agreed work plan by September 2022.
Publicity and Communications
9. Public communications related to this MOU should appropriately attribute the efforts of
both Participants, in each case subject to their consent. Each Participant intends to
respond to a communication request by the other within three business days.
Joint branding may be used with the written consent of each Participant. Each Participant
may make its logo available for use on specific materials at its sole discretion. Each
Participant should obtain written approval prior to the publication of all information and
materials that contain the other's logo. The Participants expect that any such materials
give equal prominence.
The Participants intend to respect each other's confidentiality policies, with the mutual
understanding that they publicize their alliance and its objectives without disclosing any
confidential or proprietary information of the other.
3

Each Participantmay make the existence and content of this MOU publicly availableby
press release, public commentary, or other disclosure, in accordance with their policies or
procedures regarding the public disclosure of information, subject to the prior written
consent of the other.
Reporting and Collaboration
10. The Participants understand the need for regular reporting on activities and results and
intend to collaborate to meet any intormation needs or applicable reporting requirements
in connection with the cooperation under this MOU. The participants expect any
reporting requirements, including the designation of additional points of contact and
cadence and nature of communications, to be established in the work plan.
General Provisions
11. Duration: This MOU is expected to continue for 1 year from the date of signature and
may be extended in writing. The Participants may renew or extend it by mutual written
agreement. It is understood that either Participant may terminate this MOU by giving
thirty (30) days of prior written notice to the other Participant.
12. Modifications: It is intended that the Participants may modify this MOU only in writing,
signed by both Participants.
13. Effect of MOU: This MOU is not a treaty and does not give rise to rights or obligations
under international law. The Participants specifically acknowledge that this MOU is not
an obligation of funds, nor does it constitute a legally binding commitment by any
Participant or create any rights in any third party. The Participants intend to maintain
their own separate and unique missions and mandates and their own accountabilities.
Unless specifically provided otherwise, the cooperation among the Participants as
outlined in this MOU shall not be construed as a partnership or other type of legal entity
or personality. Each Participant shall accept full and sole responsibility for any and all
expenses incurred by itself related to this MOU. Nothing in this MOU shall be construed
as superseding or interfering in any way with any agreements or contracts entered into
among the Participants, either prior to or subsequent to the signing of this MOU.
Nothing in this MOU shall be construed as an exclusive working relationship.
Points of Contact
14. The primary Points of Contact for each Participant for administering this MOU appear

Hi Matt,
Thank you for the conversation we had during our meeting in Singapore on the 23'd of April.
As we have discussed for the last couple of months, it was great to discuss possibility of
partnership with Love Frankie and its partners on running University Challenge We Think
Digital (known locally as Asah Digital) trainings on internet safety and digital literacy across
several universities in Indonesia. Below please find our minutes of conversation that we
will follow up respectively, subject to future agreements where necessary, due diligence
and also further internal approval from our end.
1. Together we will explore the possibility to support for University Challenge
Indonesia - We Think Digital with the program beginning in July 2022 - July 2023
implementation period with the following details:
• Plan to access to the latest, updated version of the WTD digital literacy materials,
total of 6 modules, developed, localized and translated together with local experts
in H1 2022, in the form of presentations and printable handouts from Program
Manager from Meta to be used during the duration of the program;
• Plan to engage Meta's current trainers, to provide trainings over the course of the
year for the duration of program;
• We may also feature the materials of the program on our WTD Website
at [link omitted] omitted]/, which will be uploaded by Meta's vendors;
• We estimate the total value of our in-kind contributions to the program (as listed
above) to be to the value of USD150,000 (exact breakdown to be discussed
together during ongoing program design discussions);
• In addition, Meta may provide ad credit coupons valued at USD30,000 to be
shared to Love Frankie to help promote the materials used together for the
program;
• We will further explore the plan to disburse USD70,000 excluding taxes to Love
Frankie in 2022, for the coordination, program development, and monitoring and
evaluation of the program;

• We will further explore the plan to renew this program in 2023-2024, subject to
future agreements where necessary and as agreed by all partners.
2. I will be in touch to discuss in more detail this prospective collaboration.
If you have input or have any questions, we will be happy to discuss further.
We thank you very much for your attention and cooperation.

USAID DISINFORMATION RESEARCH PARTNERS IN UKRAINE AND THE REGION (5/11/22)
Please find below a list of the Ukraine Mission's partners that are conducting research on
disinformation in Ukraine and the broader region.
1. Ukraine World is NGO Internews Ukraine's topical news and information resource
focusing on Ukrainian issues which brings together around 300 experts and journalists
from Ukraine and around the world. They do regular explainers and analysis of
Russian disinformation trends in the Ukrainian infosphere.
2. Detector Media is a Ukrainian NGO focusing on democratic media development,
media reforms and combating propaganda, as well as a media watchdog carrying out
reviews, in-depth analysis and critical assessments of Ukrainian TV and radio content,
and current Ukrainian media trends. Detector Media collects and documents Kremlin
disinformation around Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
3. Texty.org is a data journalism agency which focuses on studying Russian propaganda
and disinformation in the media. Texty.org developed a browser add-on called
"Fakecrunch" for Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox which allows users to report
disinformation. Texty also produces regular analysis of Russian disinformation trends.
4. VoxCheck is a fact-checking project that monitors and verifies the statements of
politicians and opinion leaders.
5. Institute of Mass Information is a Ukrainian NGO that monitors and reports on media
trends and developments in Ukraine (with a special focus on online national and
regional media), publishing a Barometer of Free Speech, reports on ethical and
professional media standards, Russian narratives, propaganda and fakes in Ukrainian
online media, reports on gender balance, hate speech, national minorities and LGBTI
coverage in media. IMI manages the Media Inclusion List: monitoring media and
producing a list of those that perform best according to professional media standards,
and therefore safe places for advertisers to promote their brands.
6. Center for Democracy and Rule of Law is a think and act tank that supports the
creation of a good legal operating environment for developing independent media,
public platforms, and movements. It develops and advocates for quality legislation,
protecting freedom of speech, and providing impartial legal expert evaluation and
advice for journalists and media companies.
7. Independent Media Council is a public advisory and expert body designed to promote
high professional standards of journalism and self-regulation in the Ukrainian media
sector by providing expert opinions. The Council considers controversial issues
regarding non-compliance with media legislation, international standards of media
coverage, as well as violations of journalistic ethics.
8. Center for Analytics and Investigations launched the fact-checking project Bez
Brekhni (Without a Lie) examining politicians' statements, and specializing in
conducting fact-checking trainings. It created the first Ukrainian rating of Politicians'
Truths and Lies.

centers.

Every day, people come to Facebook and Instagram to share their stories, see
the world through the eyes of others and connect with friends and causes. The
conversations that happen on Facebook reflect the diversity of a community of
more than two billion people communicating across countries and cultures and
in dozens of languages. We recognize how important it is for Facebook to be a
place where people feel empowered to communicate, and we take our role in
keeping abuse off our service seriously. That's why we have developed a set
of Community Standards, which govern the content that people are allowed
to share on our platforms, with the goal to encourage expression and create a
safe environment.
Background: Facebook works with trusted partner organizations who are
familiar with our policies to provide critical insights and on-the-ground
context to aid in our content moderation. We work with over 400 trusted
partners in 113 countries around the globe.
The goal of the Trusted Partner program is to establish and maintain
relationships and reporting channels with expert organizations that raise

queries and concerns about problematic content on Facebook and Instagram
to:
• address harmful content trends and prevent harm,
• foster online safety and security, and
• inform the development of fair and transparent policies.
Our partners are non-governmental organizations, human rights defenders,
humanitarian organizations, activists, or researchers that enable us to:
• learn from on-the-ground actors across the globe, especially those
representing marginalized communities,
• identify and address policy, process, or training gaps to improve the
standard report review process, and
• ensure our review of high-priority content and accounts is informed by
critical and up-to-date context.
Reporting: Our Trusted Partner Channel provides our partner organizations
with an expedited way of reporting this content to Facebook. The channel is
staffed 24/7 by a team of escalations specialists who triage reports and route
them to expert teams for analysis. Once a report is received, our team will
review the content against our Community Standards and if necessary, seek
additional context from the Trusted Partner. We will then respond back to the
Trusted Partner with our assessment. Trusted Partners are under no obligation
to report to Facebook. When Trusted Partners do report, we will only remove
the content and accounts that are in violation of our Community Standards.
Confidentiality: Given the challenging environments many of our partner
organizations work in, we keep all Trusted Partners and their reporting
practices confidential. However, partner organizations should feel free to share
the nature of our relationship and their reporting practices however they'd like.
Policy Consultations: Our team, which manages the Trusted Partner program
sits within Facebook's Content Policy team, the group that creates our
Community Standards. In the process of developing / revising our policies, we
seek input from a broad spectrum of experts and users including academics,
journalists, human rights defenders, and civil society organizations. When we
are working to develop a policy that relates to our Trusted Partner's work or
community, we reach out to see if you would be willing to discuss the subject
with us over a video conference or phone call. The feedback we receive during
these calls informs the development of fair and transparent policies that help
make our platform safer and advance freedom of expression for our users.
-
Johnny Walsh

Reporting social media content
Platforms like Facebook/Meta or Twitter are receptive to taking down content when it falls within
three categories: 1) harmful content, 2) deceptive behavior, and 3) manipulative actors. However,
reported content may not be removed or may only be deprioritized if platform adjudicators
determine that it does not violate the terms of service.
•
Harmful Content: The content needs to demonstrate violations of the platform's community
standards. Hate speech, harassment, and calls for violence usually qualify. Facebook/Meta
has set up a "court" that they call "oversight board" to adjudicate incidents, meaning that it's
not necessarily a straightforward process.
•
Deceptive Behavior: If evidence is provided, most platforms will remove content / accounts
demonstrating what Facebook calls "coordinated inauthentic behavior" (e.g., troll farms or
bots) violating their terms of service.
Manipulative Actors: In some of USAID's more developed programs, partners, specifically
investigative journalists or think tanks doing online investigations are able to map out the bad
actors on social media platforms. They use the evidence to petition the platforms to get
'inauthentic" accounts taken down. Cases are not necessarily straightforward. For example,
public figures receive more leniency to remain online in spite of violations of terms of service.
For example, AID/Georgia's Information Integrity Program described the following actions to limit
harmful content:
1. Analyze online narratives and identify actors engaging in "coordinated inauthentic
behavior". The partner will share a list of accounts with Facebook/Meta who in turn will dig
deeper and ultimately take them down or de-promote content. While this work begins
"manually" there is technology that can identify patterns that reveal the source of harmful
content. It should be noted that online content may fall under different categories
(Fake/Manipulation/Out of Context) with different levels of response. Facebook/Meta also
works with trusted organizations such as the International Network of Fact-checking
Organizations (IFCN),Graphika or the Atlantic Council's digital forensics research lab to
do the leg work and flag activities through Facebook/Meta's user interface.
2. Support local fact-checking organizations to apply adequate standards and eventually
become part of IFCN and Facebook/Meta's fact checking program. Facebook/Meta's

Trusted Partners program allows vetted partners (e.g. local CSOs) to weigh in on content
takedown requests, and for example, make determinations on whether a takedown
request is legitimate.
3. Promote benchmarks on social media advertising policies. Facebook/Meta has increased
its standards in the U.S. especially after the recent U.S. elections' claims of the site's
vulnerabilities. The program is lobbying with Facebook/Meta to introduce the same
standards overseas, especially during elections.
The above description has focused on Facebook/Meta. Working with Google, YouTube, TikTok
or Twitter has been more difficult as they are behind the curve on controlling harmful content.
Nonetheless, addressing takedown requests is incredibly complex as company decisions are
informed by their business models and local and international laws on internet governance,
among other factors. For example:
• Reporting harmful content can be abused by malign entities seeking to discredit their
adversaries.
• Facebook/Meta has decentralized and very spread out "digital threats" teams making it
difficult to
react quickly. Facebook/Meta, for example, has different enforcement
capabilities depending on the market/jurisdiction - in places where they have a strong
market presence or interest in expanding, it employs a much more robust network of
content moderators, who are fluent in local languages, meaning the policy enforcement is
extremely uneven.
• In some instances, Facebook/Metachooses not to react for fear of being exposed for
housing malicious content.
• The rules are also subject to change. Recently, for example, Facebook/Meta changed its
policy to allow users from certain Eastern European countries to call for violence against
members of the Russian government and military. This is unprecedented and raises
serious concerns.
• The machine learning models and algorithms Facebook/Meta and other social media
companies use to verify harmful content is incredibly imperfect, to the point of oftentimes
being harmful. For example, it's not uncommon for posts about atrocities or hate speech
to get flagged by an algorithm as a violation of the terms of service and get taken down,
when they are in fact posted by a journalist or human rights organization to raise the issue.
• Even in places where Facebook/Meta has hired robust
and well-trained content
moderators, these moderators frequently find themselves subject to abuse, harassment,
and threats when content moderation decisions contradict government requests.
Additionally, there are new laws being proposed and enacted by various governments that
require social media platforms to hire local staff - what some civil society groups are
terming hostage-taking laws - that could further put local staff at risk.
